newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end lower but gain on the week.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end lower but gain on the week.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices ended lower on Friday in a shortened, pre-holiday weekend session that saw the market give up a small part of its recent gains.
"It was a consolidative session," said Lee Youngdahl, economist at Aubrey G. Lanston & Co. "We had a huge run-up in a very short period of time. It took away some of the market's short base."
"The market has been up strongly over the last couple of days so we retraced that a little bit, but the tone is still positive," said Josh Feinman, economist at Bankers Trust.

Showing a 1.3 percent decline, September wholesale inventories turned out to be leaner than expected, leading economists to predict that the third-quarter 2.2 percent GDP (Gross Domestic Product) number reported recently would be revised downward. The inventories drop also implied that inventories were beneath levels that would constrain fourth quarter production if demand for new goods picked up.

"The figures suggested that there was less inventory building in the third quarter than thought," said Feinman. "They indicate inventories are pretty lean and are not going to act as a restraint on production going forward."
The notion that there is little inventory overhang to weigh on production in the fourth quarter is only one of the risks for the bond market in the months ahead, Feinman said.
"We've come a long way to settle into this new area around 6-1/2 percent on the long bond (yield)," he said. "The market is pretty comfortable here right now."
But Feinman said he would be cautious about buying bonds at these levels.
"You need to keep in mind that the labor market is quite tight and that the economy is operating with stretched resources overall," he said.
"Under such conditions, any kind of growth reacceleration carries with it inflation risks," he said.

Feinman said the market has properly concluded that the Federal Reserve will not raise interest rates this winter, but "when you get to next spring, if you get growth reaccelerating, you could very quickly be staring back down into the barrel of Fed tightening."
While the market took a step back on Friday, it hardly made a dent in an overall strong performance for the week.
The new 6-1/2 percent benchmark 30-year bond ended at 99-29/32 on Friday, down 10/32 to yield 6.51 percent.
A week earlier, the 30-year benchmark Treasury bond yield finished at 6.68 percent.

"We had a pretty good run and we're closing another week at higher prices and lower yields," said Raphael Marrone, money market economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "There was the relief trade that the U.S. election went the way the market wanted it to with the Republicans retaining control of Congress. The economic background remains favorable and we're through the (Treasury) refunding which ended with a bang with the (successful) 30-year (bond) auction."
Friday's moderate retreat was due to "some profit-taking, some backing and filling before the long holiday weekend," Marrone said.
At the close, three-month bill rates were up three basis points to 5.04 percent, six-month rates were up two basis points to 5.09 percent and year bill rates were up one basis point to 5.17 percent.
Two-year notes fell 2/32 to 100-7/32 to yield 5.75 pct. Five-year notes fell 4/32 to 100-29/32 to yield 6.04 percent.
Ten-year notes slipped 6/32 to 101-25/32, yielding 6.26 percent.
--North American Treasury Desk, 212-859-1679
